item.title: I'm a Product Manager and I Don't Read AI Agent Code. The Harness, the Process Around It, and Five Things I'll Do Differently
item.description:
The agent writes: "Done, all tests pass." Then I have two options: believe it or show it to someone who understands. There's no one to show it to. There's no developer on the project, and I don't read code myself. I'm a product manager. Since January, I've been building a Chrome extension this way. All the code was written by two AI agents, Claude Code and Codex: 593 commits and 78,478 lines of code in the product itself. Next, I'll explain how I set up checks and work with the agent: Harness. Rules, checks, prohibitions, and skills around the agent. Nine lessons with dates from the project's history. How I work with it. Six steps from idea to acceptance and the prompts I insert for the agent at each step. What I'll change in the next project. Five improvements. Each with an argument against it. This article is for two types of readers: for a manager or product manager who wants to build themselves without waiting in line for developers, and for a developer who wants to hand over a task to an agent for a few hours, trusting the result. Read more

item.title: How we launched the voice GROM live at Phystech with GPTunneL
item.description:
Three hours live at Phystech: how we tested the voice GROM with GPTunneL. At the "New Towns" hackathon in "Big Phystech," experts, schoolchildren, and students conceived a future town from scratch. The goal was to turn three hours of discussion into a one-minute video. All teams used GPTunneL to generate scenes and assemble videos, while our team simultaneously built the town's website. This all happened live, where we also tested our voice assistant based on GROM for the first time. GROM interacted with participants and summarized discussions. However, after an argument about a character's appearance, it kept bringing up his beard even in unrelated answers. I'll explain how we set up the assistant's memory, why fifteen minutes of conversation were dropped from processing, and what we managed to assemble by the end of the broadcast. Read on to find out how it all went.

item.title: LLM Chat: User Model: An Overview of Experimental Research
item.description:
In the theory of LLM chats as Luhmannian semantic systems of a new type (Krupkin, 2026), user interaction is mediated by a coupled social system, which implies that LLM/noo-systems chats can have a social role scheme of Ego-Alter communication. Here, Ego is the noo-system's role mask, how it appears to the user, and Alter is the user model in the LLM, how the LLM chat perceives the user. A search for scientific sources yields quite a few experimental LLM studies that can be linked to the Ego-Alter scheme. In particular, the fresh Habr review on the influence of even one or several LLM neurons on the noo-system's Ego concerns Ego models of LLM chats. In this review of experiments found in the literature, I will limit myself to describing the LLM chat's interlocutor – the chat user – and its modeling of the interacting Alter. Read more

item.title: Linux "Handy-man-ship"
item.description:
In October 2026, a vulnerability in the Linux kernel was patched, which could be exploited by anyone capable of sending a TCP packet. This occurred before any data reached the application, without requiring a password or account. The bug, born in January 2016, had been present for ten years, affecting nearly every TCP connection on the internet. On October 27th, Anthropic announced their unpublished model had written an exploit for it, gaining kernel access in 48 minutes and root in five more. The author argues this isn't about AI taking over, but about the cost of exploitation drastically decreasing. Two key changes have occurred: the complexity of exploiting systems has plummeted, and AI has accelerated offensive security more profoundly than development, albeit behind closed doors. The author, a CTO of a cloud provider, urges immediate action, stating that understanding C is no longer necessary to exploit such vulnerabilities, only a grasp of pointers and familiarity with languages like Go, PHP, or Node.js.

item.title: How I Almost Burned My MacBook Trying to Run an AI Agent Locally
item.description:
You know that feeling when you read an article about local LLMs and think: 'Oh, that's easy. I'll just install Ollama, pull a model, and I'll have my own AI agent that knows all the code'? I thought exactly that. My name is Egor Laptev, I'm a QA Fullstack Java at SENSE on a project for a major Russian bank. I have a MacBook Pro M2 Pro with 32GB of RAM: not a top-tier machine, but a workhorse for development. I had no idea that 20 minutes after launching the model, my laptop would sound like a fighter jet taking off, and the CPU temperature would be high enough to fry an egg on the lid. This is the story of how 'just running it locally' turned into an engineering project with a budget, calculations, and one almost-fried laptop. Read more

item.title: Book: "Deep Learning with Python, 3rd International Edition"
item.description:
Hello, Habr residents! In less than a decade, deep learning has gone through two key stages. First, Python libraries like Keras, TensorFlow, and PyTorch brought neural networks from laboratory experiments into real production. Then, LLMs and other generative AI tools transformed business and society. François Chollet, creator of the Keras library, and Matthew Watson, who works on Gemini at Google, have completely reworked and updated the book so you can understand how transformers work, build your own mini-GPT model and a diffusion image generation model, and fine-tune a language model using the LoRA method. Read more
